title: Navigation (N1)
scopeHtml: Navigation Compose and Navigation 3: back stack, type-safe routes, arguments, nested graphs, ViewModel scoping, deep links, results, multi-module patterns, predictive back, testing. Versions referenced: Navigation 2.8+ (type-safe routes; docs currently show 2.10.x), Navigation 3 (verify current stable version before quoting).

questions.promptHtml: In Navigation Compose, what are NavHost, NavController, NavGraph and NavBackStackEntry, and how do they relate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you have a mental model of the library or only copy-pasted a NavHost block. Everything else (scoping, results, deep links) hangs off these four types.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The NavController owns the back stack, a list of NavBackStackEntry objects. The NavGraph is the static map of destinations the controller can reach. NavHost is the composable that connects the two: it sets the graph on the controller and renders the composable of the top entry. Each entry carries its destination, arguments, a lifecycle, a ViewModelStore and a SavedStateHandle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• rememberNavController() creates a NavHostController and keeps it across recompositions and configuration or process recreation (it is saveable). Navigators (ComposeNavigator, DialogNavigator) are registered on it.
  • NavHost(navController, startDestination) { composable<Route> { ... } } builds a NavGraph once (the lambda is remembered against the start destination and graph arguments) and calls navController.setGraph.
  • A NavBackStackEntry is the unit of state: it is a LifecycleOwner, ViewModelStoreOwner and SavedStateRegistryOwner. This is why a ViewModel obtained inside a destination dies when its entry is popped, not when the composable leaves composition.
  • The graph is static description; the back stack is runtime state.
NavHost ──setGraph──> NavController ──owns──> back stack: [Home][List][Detail(id=7)]
                         │                         each = NavBackStackEntry
                         └── NavGraph (route -> destination map)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Serializable object Home
@Serializable data class Detail(val id: Long)

@Composable
fun AppNavHost(navController: NavHostController = rememberNavController()) {
    NavHost(navController, startDestination = Home) {
        composable<Home> { HomeScreen(onOpen = { navController.navigate(Detail(it)) }) }
        composable<Detail> { DetailScreen() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating the NavController with remember { NavHostController(context) }: it loses saved state and navigator registration.
  • Passing the NavController into leaf composables (hard to preview and test, and it hides what the screen can trigger).
  • Treating the graph as dynamic: mutating the graph per user state instead of conditional navigation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a destination's ViewModel live? → In the entry's ViewModelStore; cleared when the entry is popped for good.
  2. Can you have two NavHosts? → Yes (e.g. per tab or per pane), each with its own controller and back stack; deep links and Back handling then need explicit coordination.
  3. What happens to the composable of an entry that is not on top? → It leaves composition, but its entry (ViewModel, saved state) stays alive.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the classes. The senior explains that the entry is the lifecycle/state unit, that the graph is static while the stack is runtime, and why the controller is hoisted and not handed to leaf screens.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put NavController in every screen signature found they could not preview or unit test screens and ended up with navigation calls inside recomposition paths.

questions.promptHtml: Explain navigate(), popBackStack(), popUpTo, inclusive and launchSingleTop. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back stack bugs are the most common navigation bugs in real apps (login loops, duplicate screens, wrong Back behavior).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: navigate pushes an entry. popBackStack pops the top, or up to a given destination. popUpTo inside a navigate call pops entries before pushing; inclusive = true also removes the target itself. launchSingleTop stops a second copy of the same destination being pushed when it is already on top. Typical uses: after login, popUpTo<Login> { inclusive = true }; for tab switches, launchSingleTop plus save/restore state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without options, every navigate call pushes, so double taps or repeated deep links produce two entries of the same screen.
  • popUpTo(X) pops everything above X (X stays). inclusive = true removes X too. The pop happens in the same operation as the push, so there is no flash of the intermediate screen.
  • popBackStack() returns a Boolean: false means nothing was popped (e.g. the only entry), and the Activity should finish. It is also false when the route you asked for is not on the stack.
  • navigateUp() is "up" semantics (parent in the hierarchy, and it can leave the app to the previous app for deep links); popBackStack() is "back".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// After successful login: remove Login (and everything above it) so Back exits the app
navController.navigate(Home) {
    popUpTo<Login> { inclusive = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
}

// Remove a wizard once finished, landing on its parent
navController.popBackStack<CheckoutGraph>(inclusive = true)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using popUpTo(startDestination) with inclusive = true and then wondering why the app closes: you removed the last entry.
  • Calling navigate twice from a quick double tap with no launchSingleTop, creating duplicates.
  • Ignoring the Boolean from popBackStack(route): on a typo or a route not on the stack it silently does nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between navigateUp and popBackStack? → Up follows the graph hierarchy and may handle task boundaries; back pops the stack.
  2. What does popUpTo with a graph route do? → Pops to that nested graph's entry; inclusive removes the whole graph's entries.
  3. How would you make a splash screen not reachable by Back? → popUpTo<Splash> { inclusive = true } on the navigate away, or better, decide the start destination before building the host.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes the flags. The senior ties them to specific flows (auth, onboarding, tabs), mentions the Boolean return, and prefers not to have a splash destination at all.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login screen reachable via Back after sign-in is a classic security-review finding; the fix is one popUpTo inclusive.

questions.promptHtml: How do type-safe routes work in Navigation 2.8+, what types of arguments are supported, and how do you read them in a screen and in a ViewModel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the modern API and its limits, and whether you still write string routes with manual navArgument and "detail/{id}" concatenation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Navigation 2.8.0 a route is a @Serializable object or class from kotlinx.serialization. composable<Detail> registers it, navigate(Detail(7)) navigates, and entry.toRoute<Detail>() or savedStateHandle.toRoute<Detail>() rebuilds the object. Primitives, String, enums and lists/arrays of them work out of the box; custom types need a NavType supplied through typeMap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• At graph-build time the library derives the route pattern and the argument list from the serializer descriptor (property names, types, nullability, defaults). At navigate time it encodes the instance into the route string and the argument bundle; toRoute decodes it back.
  • Object for no-arg screens, data class for args, KClass for no-arg or all-defaulted ones.
  • Properties with defaults and nullable ones become optional arguments.
  • Custom types: pass typeMap = mapOf(typeOf<Foo>() to fooNavType) in composable<...> (and in toRoute<...>(typeMap) where needed). Passing whole domain objects is discouraged anyway (see the "what not to pass" question).
  • Needs the org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization Gradle plugin and the kotlinx-serialization-json dependency.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Serializable data class Detail(val id: Long, val source: String? = null)

composable<Detail> { entry ->
    val route = entry.toRoute<Detail>()
    DetailScreen(route.id)
}

@HiltViewModel
class DetailViewModel @Inject constructor(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: ItemRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val route = handle.toRoute<Detail>()
    val item = repo.observe(route.id)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the serialization plugin: the route class compiles but the app crashes at runtime with a missing serializer error.
  • Renaming a route property: it changes the encoded form, which breaks saved state restored by an older version and any deep link that used that name.
  • Passing large or nested objects through a custom NavType.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do optional arguments behave? → Defaulted or nullable properties are optional, in the route pattern and in deep links.
  2. How do you share a route type across modules? → Put route classes in a small api module the caller and callee both depend on (see the multi-module question).
  3. What do you do for a type Navigation does not support? → Provide a custom NavType through typeMap, or better, pass an ID and load it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "no more strings". The senior covers the typeMap escape hatch, optional args from defaults, saved-state compatibility when route classes change, and that routes are now a public contract between modules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that renamed a route field in a release saw crashes only for users restoring from process death, because their saved route used the old shape.

questions.promptHtml: What should and should not be passed as navigation arguments, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The answer separates people who know arguments live in saved state (size and staleness limits) from those who stuff models into the route.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pass identifiers and small primitives, such as a user ID, a filter enum or a mode flag, and let the destination load the data from a repository. Do not pass large objects, lists or anything that changes: arguments are serialized into a Bundle that is saved and restored, they have a size budget, and they go stale.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Arguments end up in the entry's arguments Bundle and are mirrored into the SavedStateHandle. Saved state is written into the Binder transaction on onSaveInstanceState; the process-wide buffer is about 1 MB shared by all in-flight transactions, so a big payload risks TransactionTooLargeException.
  • Data in the route is a snapshot. If the entity changes (edited elsewhere, synced), the detail screen shows stale data unless it observes the repository by ID.
  • A repository (single source of truth, cache or Room) as the shared channel gives you freshness and survives process death, because the destination only needs the ID.
  • Sensitive data (tokens, emails) in routes can leak into logs, crash reports and deep link surfaces.
  • Exceptions: small parameters that define the screen (sort order, tab index, search query) belong in the route.
Bad : navigate(Detail(product = fullProductJson))   // stale, big, saved to Parcel
Good: navigate(Detail(productId = 42))              // VM: repo.observe(42)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Serializing a list of 500 items into the route to "avoid a network call".
  • Using a singleton "bridge" object to hand data over: it dies with the process and leaks.
  • Passing a Parcelable with a lambda or Context inside.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the data is not in any repository yet (a draft)? → Write it to a draft store or a shared scoped ViewModel, pass the draft ID.
  2. Why not a shared ViewModel for everything? → Scope must be explicit (graph/entry) and it still needs restoration after process death.
  3. How big can saved state be? → Roughly 1 MB total across the transaction buffer, and less in practice (verify per OS version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "pass IDs". The senior ties it to the Binder buffer, staleness, process death and security, and names the exceptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow that passed a cart as JSON crashed intermittently on low-memory devices when backgrounded with large carts.

questions.contextHtml:
Your e-commerce app shows duplicate Order Confirmation screens for about 3% of orders, and QA sees "Back needs two presses" after checkout. Crash-free rate is fine. Code from the checkout screen:

@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(viewModel: CheckoutViewModel, navController: NavController) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    if (state.orderPlaced) {
        navController.navigate(OrderConfirmation(state.orderId))
    }
    Button(onClick = { viewModel.placeOrder() }) { Text("Pay") }
    // ... rest of UI
}

Logs show two OrderConfirmation entries in the stack on affected sessions; payment API is called once.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it only happens sometimes, and fix it so it cannot recur.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add launchSingleTop." That hides the symptom but leaves a side effect in composition and misses that state stays orderPlaced = true after Back.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it correlate with slow devices or rotation? (recomposition frequency). Is orderPlaced ever reset? (state vs event). Is the NavController passed to many screens? (design smell). Any animation on the NavHost? (the window where the screen is still composed).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add launchSingleTop = true and a popUpTo<Checkout> { inclusive = true } on that navigate call, behind a hotfix, so duplicates stop while I fix the design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) navigate is called during composition, so any recomposition while orderPlaced is true navigates again; (b) rotation or return to the screen with the state still true re-navigates; (c) the double-tap on Pay calls placeOrder twice; (d) a recomposition during the exit transition.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in navigate call site with a counter, enable recomposition counts in Layout Inspector, record steps on a slow emulator, check the entry list via navController.currentBackStack.value in a debug overlay.
  5. Root cause: A side effect runs in the composable body. Composition can run multiple times for the same state (animations, parent recomposition, config change), and orderPlaced is sticky state, so every recomposition issues another navigate. It is intermittent because it depends on how many recompositions happen before the first navigation completes.
  6. Fix: Short term: the options above. Long term: navigation is triggered by an event consumed once, from a callback or a keyed effect, and the screen takes a lambda, not the controller.
@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(
    viewModel: CheckoutViewModel,
    onOrderPlaced: (Long) -> Unit,
) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    LaunchedEffect(state.placedOrderId) {
        state.placedOrderId?.let {
            onOrderPlaced(it)
            viewModel.onOrderNavigationHandled()   // clears the field
        }
    }
    Button(onClick = viewModel::placeOrder) { Text("Pay") }
}
// NavHost: onOrderPlaced = { navController.navigate(OrderConfirmation(it)) { popUpTo<Checkout> { inclusive = true } } }
  1. Prevention: A lint/detekt rule or review checklist: no navController. calls in composable bodies; screens receive lambdas. Add a UI test that recomposes the screen and asserts the back stack size of 1.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a SharedFlow with replay for the event (it re-fires on re-collection), and I would not use a global debounce utility to paper over it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the ViewModel is cleared before the effect runs? → Then the state is lost; keep the ID in state and consume only after navigation succeeds, so a re-created screen re-navigates correctly.
  • Why not Channel-based events? → Fine with receiveAsFlow collected in a lifecycle-aware effect, but events can be dropped when the collector is gone; state-based is easier to restore.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped this exact pattern; duplicate confirmation screens inflated the "orders viewed" metric and the analytics team noticed before engineering did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only launchSingleTop, cannot say why composition re-runs.
  • Hire: identifies the side effect in composition and moves it to an effect or callback.
  • Strong hire: also fixes sticky state, discusses event consumption semantics and adds a test and lint guard.

questions.promptHtml: Compare the Navigation component with Fragments (XML graph, Safe Args) to Navigation Compose. What stays the same and what changes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most real apps are mixed; interviewers want someone who can maintain a Fragment graph and migrate it safely.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The concepts are the same: NavController, graph, destinations, back stack entries, actions, deep links. The differences are the destination type (Fragment vs composable), the graph definition (XML or Kotlin DSL vs Kotlin DSL only), argument safety (Safe Args generated classes vs type-safe route classes since 2.8) and the view lifecycle: a Fragment on the back stack keeps its instance but destroys its view, while a composable leaves composition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Fragment navigation Navigation Compose
Destination Fragment via FragmentNavigator Composable via ComposeNavigator
Graph XML (<navigation>) or Kotlin DSL Kotlin DSL (NavHost { })
Args Safe Args plugin or Bundle @Serializable routes (2.8+), or string routes
Transitions Fragment animations / Material motion AnimatedContent enter/exit lambdas
ViewModel scope by navGraphViewModels, by activityViewModels viewModel(parentEntry), hiltViewModel(entry)
Deep links <deepLink> + <nav-graph> in manifest generates intent filters navDeepLink and manual manifest intent filters
  • A Compose-only app still uses the same androidx.navigation runtime and NavBackStackEntry.
  • Mixed apps: a Fragment hosting a ComposeView navigates with the fragment's NavController and IDs/actions (type-safe Compose routes cannot be used there, per the docs); Compose screens receive lambdas.
  • Since the library moved on, programmatic graphs do not generate manifest intent filters, so you add them manually.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using viewModels() in a Fragment and viewModel() in nested Compose and getting two different instances.
  • Forgetting viewLifecycleOwner in Fragments, then leaking observers across back stack view recreation.
  • Assuming Safe Args works for Compose routes (different mechanisms).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you migrate screen by screen? → Host Compose inside Fragments first (ComposeView), then flatten into a Compose NavHost behind one feature at a time.
  2. How do deep links differ? → XML graphs generate intent filters; programmatic graphs need hand-written filters.
  3. What replaces navGraphViewModels? → viewModel(viewModelStoreOwner = graphEntry) with the entry from getBackStackEntry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Compose is simpler". Senior: concrete lifecycle differences, mixed-app bridging, ViewModel scoping API mapping and manifest/deep link differences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Half-migrated apps commonly shipped with two back stacks (Fragment manager and Compose NavHost) disagreeing about what Back does.

questions.subtopic: Back stack entry lifecycle and saved state
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the lifecycle of a NavBackStackEntry in Navigation Compose, and what survives configuration change and process death.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: State-loss bugs (lost scroll, lost form text, re-fetching on Back) all come from not knowing what lives where.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The entry has its own Lifecycle: the top entry is RESUMED, entries underneath are CREATED (their composables are out of composition), and a popped entry is DESTROYED, which clears its ViewModelStore. remember state dies when the composable leaves composition, rememberSaveable survives going to the back stack and configuration change, and SavedStateHandle plus rememberSaveable survive process death; ViewModel instances do not survive process death.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• During a transition both entries are visible: the incoming one is STARTED then RESUMED, the outgoing one drops to CREATED when the transition ends (verify exact transition states for your version; do not depend on them).
  • When you navigate from A to B, A's composable is disposed. remember values are lost; rememberSaveable values are held by a SaveableStateHolder keyed per entry and restored when A returns. That is how scroll positions with rememberLazyListState come back.
  • ViewModels attached to A stay alive in A's ViewModelStore the whole time A is on the stack, which is why Back to A shows data without a reload.
  • Process death: the NavController saves its stack (routes and arguments) via onSaveInstanceState; entries and SavedStateHandle contents are recreated, ViewModel objects are new. Anything not in SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable is gone.
            remember   rememberSaveable   VM field   SavedStateHandle
rotate        lost        kept             kept        kept
A -> B (A on stack) lost  kept             kept        kept
process death lost        kept             LOST        kept
pop A         lost        lost             cleared     lost

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun FeedScreen(vm: FeedViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()          // saveable by design
    var draft by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }  // survives A->B->back and process death
    var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }    // lost when navigating away
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding scroll state in a ViewModel field only: lost on process death.
  • Collecting flows with collectAsState in a destination and expecting it to stop when the entry is on the back stack (it stops when the composable leaves composition, but collectAsStateWithLifecycle follows the entry's lifecycle correctly).
  • Using the Activity's lifecycle in a destination for "screen visible" logic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a screen's flow collection stop? → When the composable leaves composition; collectAsStateWithLifecycle ties to LocalLifecycleOwner, which in a NavHost is the entry.
  2. How do you test process death? → Developer options "Don't keep activities" plus background and return, or adb shell am kill.
  3. What is lost if the same destination appears twice on the stack? → Each entry has its own saved state and ViewModels; they are independent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ViewModel survives rotation". Senior produces the full survival matrix and ties it to SavedStateHandle size limits and testing with kill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "search results" screen that kept the query only in the ViewModel reset to empty for users returning from background on low-RAM devices.

questions.promptHtml: How is a ViewModel scoped in Navigation Compose, and how do you scope one to a nested graph or share between two screens?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shared state across a multi-step flow is a daily problem; wrong scope means either leaks or surprising resets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: By default viewModel() or hiltViewModel() inside a composable<> uses that destination's NavBackStackEntry as the ViewModelStoreOwner, so it lives while the entry is on the back stack. To share across several screens, take the entry of their common parent graph with navController.getBackStackEntry<GraphRoute>() and pass it as the owner. The ViewModel is cleared when that entry is removed from the stack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Owner choices: entry (default), nested graph entry (shared flow), Activity (app-wide, avoid for feature state).
  • A nested graph has its own back stack entry that exists as long as any destination of the graph is on the stack; popping the last one clears the graph-scoped store.
  • Get the parent entry with remember(entry) { navController.getBackStackEntry<Graph>() }, keyed on the current entry. Without the key, a recomposition after the parent was popped (during the exit animation) throws, because the remembered lookup is stale or the call fails.
  • Hilt: hiltViewModel<VM>(viewModelStoreOwner = parentEntry) (androidx.hilt.navigation.compose).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
navigation<CheckoutGraph>(startDestination = Cart) {
    composable<Cart> { entry ->
        val parent = remember(entry) { navController.getBackStackEntry<CheckoutGraph>() }
        val shared: CheckoutViewModel = hiltViewModel(parent)
        CartScreen(shared)
    }
    composable<Payment> { entry ->
        val parent = remember(entry) { navController.getBackStackEntry<CheckoutGraph>() }
        PaymentScreen(hiltViewModel<CheckoutViewModel>(parent))
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scoping to the Activity "because it is easy": state leaks across flows and survives logout.
  • Using getBackStackEntry for a graph that is not an ancestor on the stack: IllegalArgumentException.
  • Putting UI-only state in the shared ViewModel, making it grow unbounded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a graph-scoped VM cleared? → When the graph entry is popped, i.e. all of its destinations are gone.
  2. Does popping to the start destination of the graph clear it? → No, the graph entry stays while any child remains.
  3. Alternative to graph-scoped VM? → A repository/draft store scoped via DI (session or flow scope), with each screen having its own ViewModel.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use viewModel()". Senior: explicit owner choice, key the lookup, know the clear semantics, and prefer a flow-scoped repository when the shared object becomes a god-ViewModel.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wizards sharing the Activity-scoped VM showed the previous user's half-finished form after a second visit.

questions.promptHtml: Why and when would you use nested navigation graphs in Navigation Compose, and what do they change about back stack behaviour?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Nested graphs are the main modularity tool in navigation: flows, scoping and deep link back stacks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A nested graph groups destinations that form a flow (auth, onboarding, checkout) behind one route with its own start destination. Benefits: navigate to the flow by its graph route, pop the whole flow at once, scope a ViewModel to it, hide internal routes from the rest of the app, and get the correct synthetic back stack for deep links (each level's start destination is added).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• navigation<AuthGraph>(startDestination = Login) { ... } creates a NavGraph destination; navigating to AuthGraph goes to its start destination.
  • The graph itself has an entry on the back stack, so popUpTo<AuthGraph> { inclusive = true } removes all child destinations.
  • Deep links into a child push each ancestor graph's start destination, so Back behaves like a user arriving from the entry point (per docs).
  • Graph arguments: the start destination's route arguments are needed when navigating to the graph (the graph route class carries them).
  • Modularization: each feature exposes NavGraphBuilder.featureGraph(...) so the app module composes feature graphs without seeing internals.
NavHost(navController, startDestination = Home) {
    composable<Home> { ... }
    navigation<CheckoutGraph>(startDestination = Cart) {
        composable<Cart> { ... }
        composable<Payment> { ... }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Navigating to a child directly from outside and bypassing the flow's start destination invariants.
  • Nesting too deep (4 levels): deep link synthetic stacks become surprising.
  • Same start destination class used in two graphs: route ambiguity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to leave a flow and clear it? → navigate(Home) { popUpTo<CheckoutGraph> { inclusive = true } }.
  2. Is a nested graph a separate back stack? → Same stack; a graph is an entry with children, it does not create an independent stack (unless using saveState per tab).
  3. How do you expose the flow from a feature module? → A public extension fun NavGraphBuilder.checkoutGraph(...) and a route type in an api module.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "organizes screens". Senior: clear semantics, ViewModel scope, deep link synthetic stack, module boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow without a nested graph left orphan Cart entries after payment, so Back from Order Confirmation re-entered the payment form.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app (900k DAU, 3 releases per month) has a new crash after a release that moved onboarding into a nested graph with a shared ViewModel: 0.6% of sessions, concentrated on Android 12 and 13 mid-range devices.

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: No destination with route OnboardingGraph
  is on the NavController's back stack. The current destination is ...
  at androidx.navigation.NavController.getBackStackEntry(NavController.kt)
  at com.app.onboarding.ProfileStepKt.ProfileStep(ProfileStep.kt:31)

Reports say "crashes right after finishing onboarding" and "when restoring the app". The code:

composable<Profile> { entry ->
    val parent = navController.getBackStackEntry<OnboardingGraph>()
    ProfileStep(hiltViewModel(parent), onDone = { navController.navigate(Home) { popUpTo<OnboardingGraph> { inclusive = true } } })
}
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without regressing onboarding data handling.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch" or "make the ViewModel Activity scoped". The first hides it, the second creates a state leak after logout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the trace occur on the final step (pop) or on restore? Is there an exit animation? (composition still alive after pop). Does the crash reproduce with animations disabled? What changed in the last release besides the graph?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that wraps the lookup in remember(entry) and guards with runCatching only as a stop-gap, or roll back the flag that enables the new onboarding if it is remote-controlled; check crash is reduced via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) after popUpTo(OnboardingGraph) inclusive, the Profile composable is still composed during its exit animation and recomposes; the unkeyed getBackStackEntry runs again and the graph entry is already gone; (b) restoration after process death composes the destination before the graph entry is available in that restore path; (c) wrong graph class (duplicate route name across modules); (d) Hilt component problem (red herring: the trace points to NavController).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce by slowing animations (Developer options, animator scale 10x) and finishing the flow; use Don't keep activities and kill via adb for (b); log navController.currentBackStack; check the call site line 31, which is in composition, not in a callback.
  5. Root cause: getBackStackEntry is executed in the composition body on every recomposition, with no remember key on the entry. The graph entry is removed by the pop while the exiting destination is still composed, so a recomposition looks up an entry that no longer exists. Android 12-13 mid-range devices recompose more during the longer transition frames.
  6. Fix: Key the lookup on the current entry so it is recomputed only when the entry changes, and do not read the parent after the destination started leaving.
composable<Profile> { entry ->
    val parent = remember(entry) { navController.getBackStackEntry<OnboardingGraph>() }
    val vm: OnboardingViewModel = hiltViewModel(parent)
    ProfileStep(vm, onDone = {
        navController.navigate(Home) { popUpTo<OnboardingGraph> { inclusive = true } }
    })
}

Long term: pass the ViewModel (or its state) into the step from the graph-level host and avoid per-screen lookups; or use a flow-scoped repository. 7. Prevention: UI test that finishes onboarding with animations enabled; a regression test with TestNavHostController; crash alert on IllegalArgumentException from NavController; code review rule for getBackStackEntry. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Activity scope (state survives logout); not try/catch around composition (hides real state-loss bugs).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the process was killed mid-onboarding? → Shared VM data must be in SavedStateHandle or a draft store, or the user restarts from scratch.
  • Would Navigation 3 avoid this? → It scopes ViewModels per entry via decorators, so a parent-lookup call is not needed; you pass the owner explicitly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent two weeks blaming Hilt for this trace; the actual line was a missing remember key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catches the exception or moves to Activity scope.
  • Hire: finds the recomposition during exit animation and keys the lookup.
  • Strong hire: reproduces deterministically, covers process death, adds tests and a safer long-term ownership design.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement bottom navigation with Navigation Compose so each tab keeps its own back stack, scroll position and ViewModels?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The default navigate options do not retain tab state; this is where candidates have actually built something.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Navigate to the tab with popUpTo the graph's start destination using saveState = true, plus launchSingleTop = true and restoreState = true. Saving state stores the popped entries (their back stack, saved state) and restoring brings them back. Each tab's flow is best a nested graph so the whole sub-stack is saved and restored together.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• popUpTo(start) { saveState = true } removes entries above start but stashes their state; restoreState = true restores the stashed stack for the target if it exists.
  • launchSingleTop avoids duplicate tab roots when re-tapping the same tab.
  • What is restored: back stack entries and their rememberSaveable/SavedStateHandle, not the in-memory ViewModel contents of removed entries (those are cleared when entries leave the live stack; they are recreated from saved state on restore). Verify this against your Navigation version if you rely on ViewModel instance retention.
  • A common alternative: one NavHost per tab kept alive manually. That keeps ViewModels but costs memory and breaks deep links; use only with a clear reason.
  • Re-selecting the current tab usually means "scroll to top / pop to root", implemented by you.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun NavController.navigateToTab(route: Any) = navigate(route) {
    popUpTo(graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using different popUpTo targets per tab, so saved states collide or are never restored.
  • Tabs as plain destinations (not nested graphs): restoring only the root screen, losing the sub stack.
  • Expecting ViewModel instances to be the same objects after switching tabs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why launchSingleTop? → Prevent stacking duplicates on re-select.
  2. How do you make "Back from a non-start tab go to Home"? → Because of popUpTo(startDestination), Back pops to the start tab first, then exits.
  3. Memory impact of saved tabs? → Saved state is small bundles; live entries are only on the visible stack.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: copies the snippet. Senior explains what is saved vs not, nested graphs per tab and the VM instance caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app lost its feed scroll on every tab switch for a year because restoreState was omitted.

questions.contextHtml:
Support tickets: "Switching tabs reloads the feed and loses my position" (about 8% of sessions touch tabs; feed API calls up 2.4x since the last release, p95 feed load 1.8 s). Code:

NavigationBar {
    tabs.forEach { tab ->
        NavigationBarItem(
            selected = current == tab.route,
            onClick = {
                navController.navigate(tab.route) {
                    popUpTo(navController.graph.startDestinationId)   // start only
                    launchSingleTop = true
                }
            },
            icon = { Icon(tab.icon, null) }, label = { Text(tab.label) }
        )
    }
}

Each tab is a single composable destination holding a LazyColumn with a ViewModel loading from the network on init.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you verify, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cache the feed in the ViewModel." Partly valid, but the ViewModel is being destroyed because the entry is popped; the root cause is navigation options.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it all tabs or just feed? Does it reproduce on the previous release (regression after a change in options)? Is the ViewModel init the only loader?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add saveState = true and restoreState = true. It is a two-line change that can ship as a patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) options lack save/restore, so every tab switch pops and destroys the entry and its ViewModel; (b) feed repository has no cache/dedup so each init refetches; (c) the LazyListState is not saveable (red herring if using rememberLazyListState).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log ViewModel.onCleared and init in debug; check network inspector for call counts per tab switch; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; print currentBackStack.
  5. Root cause: popUpTo without saveState discards the tab's entries; the next navigate creates a fresh entry, a new ViewModel and a new network request.
  6. Fix:
navController.navigate(tab.route) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true
}

Plus a repository cache (stale-while-revalidate) so any re-creation after process death is cheap. 7. Prevention: One shared navigateToTab helper, a UI test that scrolls, switches tabs and asserts position, and API-call-count dashboards per screen. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not an Activity-scoped feed ViewModel (state leaks); not hoisting every tab into permanent composition (memory).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the tab is a nested graph with 3 screens? → Same options restore the sub-stack too.
  • Does restoreState bring back the same ViewModel instance? → Not guaranteed; treat ViewModel as recreatable and rely on saved state and a repository cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found a 2x backend cost bump traced to this one missing flag in the tab bar.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the feed API.
  • Hire: identifies missing save/restore options.
  • Strong hire: adds cache strategy, tests and discusses ViewModel recreation.

questions.promptHtml: How do you add deep link support in Navigation Compose, and what is the difference between a deep link and an Android App Link?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep links are growth-critical (marketing, notifications) and fail in subtle manifest/verification ways.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Compose you declare deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink<Route>(basePath = ...)) on the destination, and you must add matching <intent-filter> entries yourself because programmatic graphs do not generate them. A deep link is any URI scheme mapped to your app; an App Link is an HTTPS link verified through assetlinks.json and android:autoVerify="true", so it opens the app directly without a chooser.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Matching: URI first, then action, then MIME type. Path placeholders are required; query placeholders for defaulted/nullable args are optional; extra query params are ignored.
  • Manifest needs ACTION_VIEW, DEFAULT and BROWSABLE categories and <data scheme="https" host="..." pathPrefix="..."/>.
  • App Links: host serves https://host/.well-known/assetlinks.json with your package and signing cert SHA-256; the system verifies on install (Android 12+ verification is stricter and only verified links open the app by default; verify details for your target API).
  • NavController handles the Intent via handleDeepLink; with standard launch mode this is automatic.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
composable<Profile>(
    deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink<Profile>(basePath = "https://www.example.com/profile"))
) { entry -> ProfileScreen(entry.toRoute<Profile>().id) }
<activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="www.example.com" android:pathPrefix="/profile" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring navDeepLink but no manifest filter, so the link opens the browser.
  • Missing the debug/release signing SHA-256 in assetlinks.json (verification fails only in one build type).
  • Treating deep link args as trusted input.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test? → adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://www.example.com/profile/7" and adb shell pm get-app-links <package>.
  2. Why does the link open a chooser? → Not verified or not autoVerify.
  3. What about a link requiring login? → See the auth-gated deep link scenario.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: adds navDeepLink. Senior: manifest, verification, back stack synthesis and validation of untrusted args.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Email campaign links opened the browser for 30% of users because the release signing key was missing from assetlinks.json.

questions.subtopic: Deep link back stack and launch modes
questions.promptHtml: What does the back stack look like after a deep link opens your app, and how do launchMode, FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK and onNewIntent change that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep link bugs (Back exits to the wrong place, link ignored when the app is already open) come from task and Intent mechanics, not from Navigation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With the standard launch mode the Activity is recreated for each link and the NavController handles the Intent itself, adding the start destination of every graph level beneath the target as a synthetic back stack. If the Intent carries NEW_TASK, the task is cleared and replaced. Without it, you stay in the caller's task, so Back returns to the previous app while Up goes to the parent destination. With singleTop or singleTask the Activity is reused and you must call navController.handleDeepLink(intent) in onNewIntent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Per the docs: explicit deep links (PendingIntent, notifications) clear and replace the task back stack with the destination plus each nesting level's start destination.
  • Implicit deep links follow the NEW_TASK rule above.
  • Docs strongly recommend standard launch mode with Navigation. In singleTop the existing Activity receives onNewIntent, and navigation does not auto-handle it.
  • For programmatic graphs, build explicit deep links with TaskStackBuilder.addNextIntentWithParentStack, which needs parentActivityName or manual parents.
  • The same Intent is delivered again after configuration change; Navigation tracks handled deep links so they do not repeat, but custom handling code often forgets this.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    private lateinit var navController: NavHostController
    override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
        super.onNewIntent(intent)
        navController.handleDeepLink(intent)   // needed for singleTop/singleTask
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• launchMode="singleTask" for "one instance" and then a deep link while the app is open silently does nothing.
  • Handling the deep link in onCreate manually and again via Navigation: double navigation.
  • Assuming Back from a deep-linked screen exits the app; the synthetic stack leads to the start destination.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a notification deep link different? → PendingIntent with TaskStackBuilder builds a fresh task with parents.
  2. How to skip the synthetic parents? → Handle the Intent yourself and navigate with explicit options; trade-off is non-standard Back.
  3. What if two Activities host NavHosts? → Each needs its own deep link handling and the manifest filters on the right Activity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "NavController handles it". Senior: names the three flows, the launch mode caveat and the synthetic stack rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A push campaign with singleTop MainActivity worked on cold start and failed when the app was already in the foreground.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "Order-tracking links in emails (https://shop.example.com/orders/{id}) must always land the user on the order. Some users are logged out. Some are logged in as another account. 40% of link clicks come from a cold start. We lost 18% of clicks last quarter." Today the app opens Login, and after login goes to Home, dropping the link. Security also warns that an order ID from another account must not be shown.
questions.promptHtml: Design the behaviour and implementation. What do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Check login in the destination and redirect." Loses the link after redirect, ignores account mismatch and process death during login.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What should happen if the order belongs to another account (switch or deny)? Does SSO/2FA take the user out of the app (process death risk)? Are IDs guessable (server authorisation)? Should the link survive an app update and restart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Persist the pending link before redirecting so clicks are not lost; this alone recovers most of the 18%.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the 18%): (a) pending link dropped after login; (b) cold start race: link handled before session is restored; (c) login in browser/custom tab returns via another Intent; (d) link not verified, so users hit the browser.
  4. How I'd verify each: Funnel events (link opened, login shown, order shown); adb link tests in logged in/out; kill the app mid-login.
  5. Root cause: No state machine ties the link to the post-auth destination; the data is only in a transient Intent.
  6. Fix: Treat the deep link as a pending destination in a small DeepLinkCoordinator/session-scoped holder persisted via SavedStateHandle or DataStore. Gate: the navigation graph has an auth nested graph; the start destination is chosen from session state (loading, authed, unauthed). After auth, consume the pending link and navigate with popUpTo<AuthGraph> { inclusive = true }. Server returns 403/404 for another account's order; the screen shows "Not your order, switch account" with a clear action. Do not render data before the authorisation response.
  7. Prevention: UI tests for four states (cold/warm × in/out), analytics funnel, no sensitive data in link params, rate-limit order lookups.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not an in-memory singleton (lost on process death); not auto-switching accounts silently; not putting auth checks only on the client.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Link arrives while the user is mid-checkout? → Ask product; I'd show a confirmation or push it on top, never silently discard checkout state.
  • Expiry of the stored link? → Keep it a short TTL (e.g. 15 minutes), a stale link after a day is surprising.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team recovered 11 points of link conversion by persisting the pending link; the biggest bug was process death during a banking app redirect.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: redirects to login and forgets the link.
  • Hire: persists the pending link, handles cold start.
  • Strong hire: covers account mismatch, server authorisation, process death, funnel metrics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you return a result from one screen to the previous one in Navigation Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Replaces startActivityForResult; shows if you understand saved state on entries versus shared state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Before popping, the child writes to the previous entry's SavedStateHandle: navController.previousBackStackEntry?.savedStateHandle?.set("key", value). The parent reads it from its own currentBackStackEntry.savedStateHandle, usually via getStateFlow or getLiveData, then clears it. Values must be Bundle-saveable. For richer data, a shared repository or graph-scoped ViewModel is better.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The previous entry's SavedStateHandle is saved with its entry, so the result survives process death only if the value is saveable (primitives, Parcelable, Serializable).
  • The result is consumed state, not an event: remove it after reading or you will re-handle it after rotation.
  • Alternatives: result callbacks via a shared graph ViewModel; a repository (e.g. selected address stored in a draft); Navigation 3 has a documented pattern for returning results (check its docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Child
navController.previousBackStackEntry?.savedStateHandle?.set("picked_country", code)
navController.popBackStack()

// Parent destination
val handle = entry.savedStateHandle
val picked by handle.getStateFlow<String?>("picked_country", null).collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
LaunchedEffect(picked) { picked?.let { vm.onCountryPicked(it); handle["picked_country"] = null } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a non-saveable object (lambda, large list) into the handle.
  • Not clearing the key; result re-applied after config change.
  • Using currentBackStackEntry instead of previousBackStackEntry in the child (it writes to itself).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about dialog destinations? → Same API; previous entry is the screen under the dialog.
  2. Why not a global SharedFlow? → Lost if no collector, not restored after process death.
  3. Result across several screens? → Graph-scoped ViewModel or a repository.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: shows the snippet. Senior: consumption, saveability and the alternative of a shared store.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Country picker results re-applied on every rotation and reset the form a user was filling.

questions.contextHtml:
Address picker flow: Checkout -> AddressList -> AddAddress. After saving, AddAddress sets the new address ID on the previous entry and pops. Reports: 1.2% of users on 3GB RAM devices lose the new address and see the old one; sometimes "ghost" addresses are applied twice after rotation. Code:

// AddAddress
navController.previousBackStackEntry?.savedStateHandle?.set("new_address", address)  // data class AddressUi (not Parcelable)
navController.popBackStack()

// AddressList
val result = entry.savedStateHandle.get<AddressUi>("new_address")
if (result != null) { vm.select(result) }

Logs: IllegalArgumentException: Can't put value with type class AddressUi into saved state on some paths.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it Parcelable" only. That fixes the crash but not the repeated application and not the lost-on-kill case.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When does the crash occur (on save of state, at background)? Does the AddressUi include large fields? Is the address already persisted server-side before returning?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return only the address ID (a String) and make AddressList observe the repository; hotfix removes the non-saveable object.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) non-saveable object in SavedStateHandle: saved state serialisation fails or drops it on process death (the exception appears when state is saved/validated); (b) result never consumed, so reapplied on every recomposition or rotation (the ghost applies); (c) select runs in composition each time; (d) race with background refresh (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Don't keep activities repro; log reads of the key; unit test the ViewModel with SavedStateHandle.
  5. Root cause: The handle is a restoration mechanism, not an in-memory channel. A non-saveable value works until the process dies or state is saved and a result is treated as persistent state that is never cleared.
  6. Fix: Return an ID, clear after reading, and persist the entity first so the list only needs to refresh.
// AddAddress: save to repo first, then
navController.previousBackStackEntry?.savedStateHandle?.set("new_address_id", id)
// AddressList
val id by entry.savedStateHandle.getStateFlow<String?>("new_address_id", null).collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
LaunchedEffect(id) { id?.let { vm.select(it); entry.savedStateHandle["new_address_id"] = null } }
  1. Prevention: Lint for non-primitive handle writes; tests that kill the process; a small ResultKey<T> helper limited to saveable types.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a singleton event bus; not passing the whole object.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two screens returning results simultaneously? → Distinct keys per request; or a request ID.
  • Compose recomposition race with the pop animation? → Reads are from state flows, so they are idempotent after clearing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found the crash only in the monthly low-memory device cohort; the ghost applies had been blamed on the backend for weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: makes it Parcelable and stops.
  • Hire: IDs plus clearing consumed state.
  • Strong hire: persistence-first design, process death testing, guard rails.

questions.promptHtml: How do you structure navigation in a multi-module app where feature modules must not depend on each other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Navigation is the hidden coupling between features; the answer shows architectural judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each feature owns its destinations. Route types that others need live in a thin api/navigation module, and the feature's impl exposes NavGraphBuilder.featureGraph(...) and NavController.navigateToFeature(...) extension functions. The app module (or a navigation module) wires graphs together and passes callbacks, so features navigate by calling lambdas or interface methods, never by depending on another feature's UI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pattern in Now in Android style: a feature navigation source set has the route class, a navigateTo... extension, and a ...Screen graph builder; the app depends on all features and builds the NavHost.
  • Option A: routes in a shared :navigation or per-feature :api modules (cheap, type-safe, still a dependency edge to the api only).
  • Option B: String/URI-based navigation through deep link style routes (no compile-time dependency; loses type safety).
  • Option C: an app-level Navigator interface in a core module, implemented in :app; features call navigator.openOrder(id).
  • Key constraint: no feature-to-feature dependency, no cycles, and api modules contain only types.
:feature:orders:api  (OrdersRoute)   <- :feature:cart:impl uses it
:feature:orders:impl (ordersGraph)   <- :app wires
:app: NavHost { ordersGraph(onOpenCart = { nav.navigate(CartRoute) }) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A giant :navigation module holding every route: any route change recompiles everything.
  • Passing the NavController into feature modules: they can navigate anywhere.
  • Hardcoded string routes in two modules, drifting silently.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Impact on build time? → api modules are tiny and stable; impl changes do not invalidate dependents.
  2. How do you handle dynamic feature modules? → Deep link or interface lookup since compile-time deps are impossible.
  3. How do you prevent violations? → Dependency graph checks (Gradle rules, Konsist or similar).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: a single navigation module. Senior: api/impl split, lambdas for outward edges, build-time impact and enforcement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team's :navigation module changed daily and invalidated 60% of the build cache.

questions.contextHtml: Your app has 40 modules, 120 string routes like "order/{id}?src={src}", 1.5M DAU, deep links from push and email (20% of sessions), and a 2-week release train. A few modules call navigate("order/$id") from other modules via copy-pasted strings. You want type-safe routes (Navigation 2.8+) with zero deep link regression and a gradual rollout.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do it in one big PR over a weekend." Breaks deep links, saved state and releases.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a deep link inventory? Can we hold feature freeze for modules? Do we have telemetry on deep link successes? Which Navigation version are we on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not needed (no incident); I'd freeze new string routes.
  3. Hypotheses (risks), ranked: deep link patterns changing, saved state compatibility for restored sessions, argument naming mismatches, nullable/default semantics, cross-module string usage.
  4. How I'd verify: Golden tests that list every deep link URL and assert resolution; compare old and new route patterns; instrumented restore tests.
  5. Root cause: Strings are an implicit contract between modules; the migration must preserve the external ones (deep links) while replacing the internal ones.
  6. Fix (plan): (1) Upgrade Navigation first with no behaviour change. (2) Add the serialization plugin. (3) Migrate leaf modules first: add @Serializable route, register composable<Route>, keep the old string deep link in navDeepLink (use the same URI pattern; name properties as the old placeholder names). (4) Provide navigateTo...(...) extension functions per module and replace string callers. (5) Remove old string registration once callers are gone. Both styles can coexist in one NavHost during the transition (verify mixed-use against your version).
  7. Prevention: A lint rule banning navigate(String); a deep link regression suite; staged rollout with deep link success rate monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big bang; not changing external URL shapes; not renaming route fields in the same release as the migration.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users restore from a saved state written by the old version? → Process death across an app update is rare (process is killed on update) so risk is low; still test it.
  • A module needs a custom type? → Replace with an ID first, otherwise typeMap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team broke email deep links because an optional query parameter was now required; the golden URL tests caught it in CI the second time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big bang.
  • Hire: incremental, leaf first, protects deep links.
  • Strong hire: lint enforcement, golden tests, rollout metrics and saved state analysis.

questions.promptHtml: How do transitions work in Navigation Compose, and what are the pitfalls with shared elements and nested graphs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Transitions affect perceived performance and expose lifecycle details (both screens are composed at once).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NavHost is built on AnimatedContent. You supply enterTransition, exitTransition, popEnterTransition, popExitTransition at the host, graph or destination level. During the animation both destinations are composed, so each must tolerate being visible together. Shared element transitions are supported through SharedTransitionLayout with AnimatedVisibilityScope from the destination (API availability depends on your Compose version; verify).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Transitions run on the composition and the entry lifecycle: incoming is STARTED then RESUMED; outgoing leaves composition after the exit animation completes.
  • Heavy composables doubling at once cost frames: avoid expensive layout in both.
  • Nested graph transitions apply to destinations inside, with inner overriding outer.
  • Predictive back runs the pop transitions interactively on supported versions.
  • Reducing risk: avoid launching network calls triggered by composition during the animation; load in the ViewModel.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
NavHost(
    navController, startDestination = Home,
    enterTransition = { slideIntoContainer(AnimatedContentTransitionScope.SlideDirection.Start, tween(300)) },
    exitTransition = { fadeOut(tween(150)) },
    popEnterTransition = { fadeIn(tween(150)) },
    popExitTransition = { slideOutOfContainer(AnimatedContentTransitionScope.SlideDirection.End, tween(300)) },
) { /* destinations */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Different durations leaving a frame with a blank background; set a window/surface background.
  • Reading state of the previous destination inside the next one's animation.
  • Animating with Modifier.animateContentSize simultaneously, causing jank on low-end devices.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you disable animation in tests? → Set the mainClock or provide EnterTransition.None for test hosts.
  2. How do you override per destination? → Pass transition lambdas to composable<...>.
  3. Where does jank come from? → Double composition and layout during the transition; profile with Perfetto/JankStats.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "pass enterTransition". Senior: lifecycle during transition, cost, background colours, predictive back interplay.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A p95 frame time spike on low-end devices came from two heavy screens composing simultaneously during a 400 ms slide.

questions.contextHtml:
After targeting Android 15 (API 35) QA reports: on the Edit Profile screen the predictive back gesture shows no preview animation and the "Discard changes?" dialog flashes after the app already left the screen. On Android 12 devices the screen works. Code:

@Composable
fun EditProfileScreen(vm: EditVm, onExit: () -> Unit) {
    val dirty by vm.dirty.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    BackHandler(enabled = true) {
        if (dirty) vm.showDiscardDialog() else onExit()
    }
    // ...
}

Manifest has no enableOnBackInvokedCallback attribute on the <application>. The screen is inside a NavHost.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you make back handling correct?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Predictive back is a system feature, nothing to do." Misses both opt-in and enabled handling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which targetSdk and Navigation/Compose versions? Is the system setting on? Do other screens show previews? Are there custom onBackPressed overrides?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the handler's enabled follow the dirty state so the system default (and preview) applies when there is nothing to guard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) BackHandler(enabled = true) always intercepts, so the system cannot play the default animation; (b) the app is not opted into android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback (opt-in is needed on 13-14; behaviour on 15 follows the platform default for the target, verify details); (c) the dialog is shown after the transition because the handler runs on gesture commit, not during it; (d) legacy onBackPressed override (red herring unless present).
  4. How I'd verify: Developer options "Predictive back animations", Android Studio Logcat for OnBackInvokedCallback, a debug screen that logs registered callbacks, lint warnings about back handling.
  5. Root cause: An always-enabled interceptor opts the whole screen out of system back animations and runs custom logic at commit time.
  6. Fix:
BackHandler(enabled = dirty) { vm.showDiscardDialog() }   // not dirty: system/NavHost handles back

Manifest:

<application android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" ...>

For custom animation while guarding, use PredictiveBackHandler { progress: Flow<BackEventCompat> -> ... } (collect progress; completion means committed). 7. Prevention: Test Back on a predictive-capable device in QA; keep handlers conditional; avoid onBackPressed overrides. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not disabling predictive back app-wide; not listening to Back via key events.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Nested handlers? → Last registered enabled wins; deeper composables take precedence.
  • Does NavHost support predictive back? → Navigation Compose 2.8+ adds seekable predictive back transitions (verify exact version and API for your setup).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found half the app lacked previews because a base screen wrapper registered a permanent BackHandler for analytics.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ignores enabled and opt-in.
  • Hire: conditional handler and manifest flag.
  • Strong hire: PredictiveBackHandler, test plan, and awareness of version differences.

questions.promptHtml: What is Navigation 3, how does it differ from Navigation 2.x, and when would you adopt it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests currency and the ability to evaluate a new foundational library critically.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Navigation 3 is a new library built for Compose where the app owns the back stack as an observable list of keys and NavDisplay renders it. There is no NavController or XML graph: you add and remove keys, and an entryProvider maps each key to content. Scoping (ViewModel, saved state) comes from entry decorators; adaptive multi-pane layouts come from scene strategies. Check the current stable status and version before committing; the official docs and nav3-recipes repo are the reference.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Back stack: a snapshot-backed list (SnapshotStateList) of keys; rememberNavBackStack supports serializable keys that survive configuration and process death.
  • NavDisplay(backStack, entryProvider = entryProvider { entry<Home> { ... } }) renders the top entry; it can show more than one entry at a time with scenes (list-detail).
  • Decorators: rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator and rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator give per-entry saveable state and ViewModels; a ViewModel is created when the entry is added and cleared when removed.
  • Navigation logic is plain list manipulation: backStack.add(Detail(7)), backStack.removeLastOrNull(); testable without Android.
  • Trade-offs: you write more of the behaviour (multi-stack tabs, result passing, deep link parsing) yourself, ecosystem and docs are younger, and migration from 2.x is manual. Official docs list deep links, return results and animations as dedicated topics.
@Serializable data object Home : NavKey
@Serializable data class Detail(val id: Long) : NavKey

@Composable
fun App() {
    val backStack = rememberNavBackStack(Home)
    NavDisplay(
        backStack = backStack,
        onBack = { backStack.removeLastOrNull() },
        entryProvider = entryProvider {
            entry<Home> { HomeScreen(onOpen = { backStack.add(Detail(it)) }) }
            entry<Detail> { DetailScreen(it.id) }
        },
    )
}

(Verify artifact names and API signatures against the current Navigation 3 release.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the ViewModel decorator and sharing ViewModels incorrectly.
  • Mutating a non-snapshot list.
  • Assuming 2.x features (nested graph scoping, popUpTo options) exist one to one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do bottom tabs? → Multiple back stacks you manage (a top-level key list plus per-tab stacks); official recipes show patterns.
  2. How do you test navigation? → Assert on the list; no controller needed.
  3. Do you migrate an existing 2.x app? → Not by default; new Compose-only features first, weigh the cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "newer, uses a list". Senior: ownership model, scoping decorators, scenes and an adoption stance with risks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams hit by controller-state bugs (back stack out of sync with UI state) find "the back stack is just your state" appealing.

questions.contextHtml: A 600k DAU Compose-heavy app (70% Compose, 30% Fragments in 4 legacy flows, 25 modules) is about to build a tablet/foldable list-detail experience. The tech lead proposes migrating everything to Navigation 3 this quarter. You have 6 Android engineers, a monthly release, and a crash-free target of 99.7%.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "New is better, migrate everything" or "Never touch it, it works."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the adaptive requirement actually need (two-pane only or fully custom scenes)? Which Navigation 3 version/status is current and what is its support commitment? How much custom navigation code exists (tabs, results, deep links)? What is the cost of the Fragment flows?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would timebox a spike.
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked: (a) stay on 2.x and implement two-pane with adaptive layouts inside a destination; (b) adopt Navigation 3 for new Compose-only features and keep 2.x elsewhere; (c) full migration.
  4. How I'd verify: A one-week spike of a vertical slice (list-detail, deep link, result, bottom tab, process death restore) on Nav 3 using the recipes repo; compare lines of code, test ergonomics, crash behaviour.
  5. Root cause (of the decision): The business value is the adaptive layout; Navigation 3's multi-destination scenes target it, but the Fragment flows and custom tab/result logic make a full migration expensive.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Option (b) behind a module boundary if the spike passes: new adaptive features use Nav 3 with a bridge (a Compose host inside the legacy graph via a single route); leave stable 2.x flows alone; revisit full migration after a release or two.
  7. Prevention: Keep navigation behind per-feature interfaces (callbacks/route types), so the host library is swappable; record the decision and exit criteria.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a quarter-long migration on a monthly release; not mixing two controllers without a clear bridge; not adopting on a version I have not verified as stable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership wants it "for hiring appeal"? → Not a reason by itself; the spike data should drive it.
  • Two back stacks disagree during the transition? → Define one owner per screen area and a single entry point for Back.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team kept routes and screens library-agnostic so their later host swap touched one module.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-in or never.
  • Hire: incremental, spike-based.
  • Strong hire: swap-friendly boundaries, explicit exit criteria, verifies stability.

questions.contextHtml:
CI has a flaky UI test (fails 1 in 12 runs, 4% of the suite's failures):

@Test fun tapOrder_opensDetail() {
    lateinit var navController: TestNavHostController
    composeRule.setContent {
        navController = TestNavHostController(LocalContext.current)
        AppNavHost(navController)
    }
    composeRule.onNodeWithText("Order #7").performClick()
    assertEquals("detail", navController.currentDestination?.route)
}

After moving to type-safe routes the test asserts a string that no longer exists, and sometimes currentDestination is null.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it flake, and how should navigation be tested at each level?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Thread.sleep" or "Use Espresso idle waits".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the test attach ComposeNavigator? Are transitions enabled? Is the assertion on UI content or controller state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the test or quarantine it while fixing; do not retry-until-green.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the controller does not have ComposeNavigator added and the graph is not set before assertion (null destination); (b) the route string no longer matches type-safe routes (route is the serial-name based pattern); (c) assertion races with the transition; (d) the test controller is recreated on recomposition (it is created inside setContent).
  4. How I'd verify: Run 50 repetitions; log currentBackStackEntry; check composeRule.waitForIdle() usage.
  5. Root cause: The controller is created in composition (recreated), and the destination is checked by an obsolete string, with no synchronization after the click.
  6. Fix:
@Test fun tapOrder_opensDetail() {
    val navController = TestNavHostController(ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext()).apply {
        navigatorProvider.addNavigator(ComposeNavigator())
    }
    composeRule.setContent { AppNavHost(navController) }
    composeRule.onNodeWithText("Order #7").performClick()
    composeRule.waitForIdle()
    assertTrue(navController.currentBackStackEntry?.destination?.hasRoute<Detail>() == true)
    assertEquals(7L, navController.currentBackStackEntry?.toRoute<Detail>()?.id)
}

Test levels: unit test the ViewModel emitting navigation state; screen tests with lambdas (onOpen recorded) and no NavController; a few end-to-end tests with a real NavHost; deep link tests via Intent. 7. Prevention: Screens take lambdas so most tests need no controller; one shared test rule creates the controller; run flaky tests repeatedly in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not asserting on rendered text of the next screen only (hides graph errors); not mocking NavController everywhere (brittle).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you test deep links? → Launch the Activity with a VIEW Intent and assert the destination and back stack.
  • How do you test graph-scoped ViewModels? → Provide a ViewModelStore to the test controller (setViewModelStore).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team cut navigation test flake to zero by moving 90% of assertions to lambda-based screen tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeps and retries.
  • Hire: proper TestNavHostController setup and type-safe assertions.
  • Strong hire: layered test strategy and deep link/back stack tests.

questions.contextHtml: Your phone-first app (Compose, Navigation 2.8+) must support tablets and foldables: tablets are 9% of users but 22% of revenue. List-detail should show both panes when the window is wide, and on a phone navigate to detail as a separate screen. Foldables change posture and window size at runtime, and users rotate while detail is open. A prototype used if (isTablet) to pick between two different NavHosts; QA finds lost selection on fold, double back stacks and deep links landing on the wrong pane.
questions.promptHtml: How would you design the navigation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Check isTablet (resources) and use a different NavHost." Breaks on fold/resize and multi-window.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which window size classes must be supported? Should selection survive resize? Do deep links target the detail pane? Is there multi-window/desktop mode?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove device-class checks; drive layout by the current window size class and keep one back stack.
  3. Hypotheses (causes of QA bugs), ranked: two NavHosts with separate state; selection kept in remembered local state; layout switching destroys composition; deep link only understood by one host.
  4. How I'd verify: Resize emulator, foldable emulator posture changes, Layout Inspector, process death tests.
  5. Root cause: Navigation state tied to a layout instead of the app's logical state.
  6. Fix: Model logical navigation as one back stack of destinations (List, Detail(id)).
