Layout decides presentation: in a compact window Detail is a separate destination; in an expanded window the list-detail layout shows List with Detail's content beside it (Material3 adaptive NavigableListDetailPaneScaffold, or Navigation 3 scenes/list-detail strategy; verify artifact names). Selection lives in saved state (the route's ID), not local remember. Deep link to Detail yields back stack [List, Detail(id)] on any size; the layout presents it as two panes when wide.
  7. Prevention: Screenshot/UI tests across window size classes, resize tests, a fold test in CI device farm.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Device-type resource qualifiers for logic; not two parallel navigation implementations.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User opens Detail on phone then unfolds? → Same back stack; layout now shows two panes with the Detail selected.
  • Is Navigation 3 needed? → Not required; it makes multi-destination layouts a first-class feature, a reason to evaluate it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team rebuilt tablet navigation twice before accepting that the back stack must be layout-independent.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: device checks.
  • Hire: window size classes, one back stack.
  • Strong hire: logical vs presentation split, deep links, state restoration, test matrix.

questions.promptHtml: How should a ViewModel trigger navigation in a Compose app: events, state, or direct NavController access?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common architectural debate; shows understanding of UDF, event loss and testability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The ViewModel should not hold the NavController. It exposes state that includes a navigation request (or outcome), and the UI consumes it with a keyed effect, calls a navigation lambda, then tells the ViewModel the request was handled. This is restorable and cannot be lost or doubled the way a one-shot SharedFlow or Channel can.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Direct controller access ties ViewModel to UI, leaks the controller and breaks tests.
  • One-shot event streams (SharedFlow without replay, Channel) can drop events when no collector is active (during configuration change or stop) or, with replay, re-fire.
  • Modelling navigation as state (val navigation: NavTarget?) makes the event durable until consumed and testable (assert state).
  • Trade-offs: needs an explicit "handled" call; state must be cleared exactly once.
  • Alternative accepted in practice: a Channel(BUFFERED) collected in a lifecycle-aware effect, documenting that events during stop are queued.
class CheckoutViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutUi())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()
    fun onPaid(id: Long) = _ui.update { it.copy(navigateTo = OrderConfirmation(id)) }
    fun onNavigated() = _ui.update { it.copy(navigateTo = null) }
}

LaunchedEffect(ui.navigateTo) {
    ui.navigateTo?.let { onNavigate(it); vm.onNavigated() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Collecting a SharedFlow with collectAsState in composition and navigating in the body.
  • Never clearing the state: Back re-navigates.
  • Navigating before the screen is resumed during a transition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not pass NavController to the VM? → Lifecycle mismatch, leak, untestable.
  2. Where does validation like auth gating belong? → Domain/session state driving the start destination or a redirect, not scattered checks.
  3. Which approach does the official guidance prefer? → UI events modelled as state and consumed by the UI (verify the current architecture guide wording).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use SharedFlow". Senior: failure modes of each mechanism and the consume-after-navigate contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dropped one-shot event during rotation left users staring at a spinner after a successful payment.
